title: Bash API
text:
Bash API

Generated from public function usage comments in clyops.sh.

 info

Usage: info <message...>. Log an informational message to stderr.

 warn

Usage: warn <message...>. Log a warning to stderr.

 error

Usage: error <message...>. Log an error to stderr.

 success

Usage: success <message...>. Log a success message to stderr.

 die

Usage: die <exit_code> <message>

 clyops_name

Usage: clyops_name <name>. Set the program name for help and completion.

 clyops_root

Usage: clyops_root <directory>. Set the base for default and environment paths.

 clyops_description

Usage: clyops_description <text>. Set the description below the usage line.

 clyops_epilog

Usage: clyops_epilog <text>. Set the final help text.

 clyops_command

Usage: clyops_command "<word> [<word>...]" <description>
Registers a command (spec section 1.7); later registrations belong to it.
"db migrate" is the migrate command of db, which must be registered first.

 clyops_effects

Usage: clyops_effects <effect>...   (read-only, idempotent, destructive, network)

 clyops_stdin

Usage: clyops_stdin <description> [content-type]   /   clyops_stdout <description> [content-type]

 clyops_stdout

Usage: clyops_stdout <description> [content-type]. Declare output metadata.

 clyops_role

Usage: clyops_role <name> <in|out> <description> [content-type] [schema-json]
Declare a role (spec section 1.3): a stream on a descriptor the runner chooses. name: meta,
progress, log, result or another agreed name; schema-json: a JSON Schema each document or line matches.

 clyops_fd_open

Usage: clyops_fd_open <role>
Prints the descriptor for a declared role and succeeds when CLYOPS_FDS maps it and it is open
(spec section 14); fails silently otherwise.

 clyops_emit

Usage: clyops_emit <role> <text>
Write text and a newline (unless it ends with one) to a declared "out" role (spec section 14).
Does nothing when the runner didn't map it; write errors are ignored.

 clyops_forward_fds

Usage: clyops_forward_fds <role>...
Prints the CLYOPS_FDS value passing these roles on to a program this one starts (spec section 14).

 clyops_exclusive

Usage: clyops_exclusive <long>...  /  clyops_requires <long> <long>...  /  clyops_one_of <long>...

 clyops_requires

Usage: clyops_requires <long> <long...>. The first option requires the others.

 clyops_one_of

Usage: clyops_one_of <long...>. Require at least one listed option.

 clyops_config

Usage: clyops_config <option-long-name> <prefix[,prefix...]>

 clyops_require_command

Usage: clyops_require_command <command> <description> [install-hint]

 clyops_path_search

Usage: clyops_path_search <long> <dir[:dir...]>   (dirs relative to the root)

 clyops_opt

Usage: clyops_opt <VAR> <long> <short> <default|flag|optional|""> <description> [group] [rule]

 clyops_opt_array

Usage: clyops_opt_array <VAR> <long> <short> <description> [group] [rule]

 clyops_arg

Usage: clyops_arg <NAME> <description> [default] [rule]

 clyops_arg_variadic

Usage: clyops_arg_variadic <NAME> <description> [rule]

 clyops_parse

Parse without exiting. Returns 0 when values were assigned; otherwise
_CLYOPS_HELP is set (help requested) or _CLYOPS_ERROR holds the message.

 clyops_run

Parse like a CLI: handles --help, --help-json-schema and --bash-completion,
prints errors and exits on failure, otherwise assigns the variables.

 clyops_source

Print where an option's value came from: cli, config, env, default or unset.

 clyops_is_set

Usage: clyops_is_set <long>. Return zero if the option came from CLI, else one.

 clyops_is_explicitly_set

Usage: clyops_is_explicitly_set <long>. Return zero for CLI/config/env, else one.

 clyops_values_json

Resolved values as JSON (spec section 10).

 clyops_usage

Help text (spec section 7), for the selected command.

 clyops_json_schema

JSON description of the CLI (spec section 8).

 clyops_completion_data

Tab-separated completion records (spec section 9). The arguments are the
words typed after the program name; a program with commands follows them.

 clyops_completion_script

Print a script that enables completion for this program in bash, zsh or fish
(spec section 9): eval "$(prog --completion bash)". Returns 1 for an unknown shell.

title: Dispatcher and desktop runner
text:
Dispatcher and desktop runner

 Dispatcher

clyops-dispatch turns a directory into nested subcommands. Download a binary
from the [release](https://github.com/wankdanker/clyops/releases), then:

sh
clyops-dispatch --root ./tools --name mytools --help
clyops-dispatch --root ./tools --name mytools media convert --help


A .clyops file controls descriptions, directories, ignored entries and allowed
or denied tools. Source detection requires a supported import/source statement
or an explicit  clyops-tool / // clyops-tool header marker for wrappers.
Binary completion markers and nested dispatcher shebangs are also supported.
Schemas are cached by file stamp; probes have a timeout.

The [dispatcher guide](../apps/dispatch/README.md) covers definition files,
aliases, completion, caching and filesystem behavior. This application exposes
a command-line interface, rather than an installed library API.

 Desktop runner

The runner lists tools and generates forms from their schemas, including commands,
secrets, constraints, effect badges and declared stdin/stdout. Unchecked flags
explicitly override enabled config/environment values. Templates preserve false
and zero values and omit secrets. Destructive tools require confirmation. A tool's
progress role shows as a progress bar, its meta beside the output, and log
and result lines in it.

See the [runner guide](../apps/runner/README.md) for installation, usage, templates
and frontend/native development. Its internal UI helpers are not a public package API.

 Documentation (clyops-doc)

clyops-doc reads a tool's --help-json-schema and writes a man page, Markdown or HTML, so any
clyops tool gets documentation without writing it twice:

sh
mytool --help-json-schema | clyops-doc > mytool.1
mytool --help-json-schema | clyops-doc --format markdown --name "mytool media to-pcm" > to-pcm.md


A program with commands gets a section per command with the options it inherits. To write files
instead, give --out-dir (or --prefix to install man pages where man looks), and --execute
to actually write them; without it, clyops-doc only lists the files:

sh
mytool --help-json-schema | clyops-doc --split --out-dir man1 --execute     mytool.1, mytool-db-migrate.1, ...
clyops-doc --root ./tools --name mytools --prefix ~/.local --execute        every tool, and an index page


--split gives each command a page of its own, git-style, and --root documents a whole directory
of tools the way the dispatcher finds them. The [clyops-doc guide](../apps/doc/README.md) covers
the options and what goes in each section; [spec section 15](../spec/SPEC.md15-documentation-clyops-doc)
is the contract.

 Web runner

The static SvelteKit web runner is served by clyops-api at /ui/. It discovers
tools through REST and uses the shared schema package for typed fields, ranges,
relationship hints and secret handling. See the [web runner guide](web-runner.md).

title: Bash, Zsh and Fish completion
text:
Bash, Zsh and Fish completion

Every clyops tool generates its own shell completion. Options, enum values, file
and directory paths, hosts, nested commands and inherited options come from the
tool's current declarations. No hand-maintained completion file is needed when
you change its options.

For a tool installed on PATH, replace plan.py below with its executable name.
To use the [cloned examples](examples.md), first run the PATH setup from your
shell while you are in the repository root. These commands enable the current
shell session. Put PATH and initialization lines in your startup file to retain
them, using the absolute checkout path rather than $PWD there.

 Bash

Use Bash 4.3+; on macOS put a current Bash on PATH and start it first.

bash
export PATH="$PWD/examples/scripts:$PATH"
eval "$(plan.py --completion bash)"


Type plan.py --env  and press Tab to complete staging or production.

For future sessions, add to ~/.bashrc after adjusting the checkout path:

bash
export PATH="/absolute/path/to/clyops/examples/scripts:$PATH"
eval "$(plan.py --completion bash)"


Your login shell may need to source ~/.bashrc from ~/.bash_profile.
The generated function queries the executable when you complete; keep the tool
on PATH and use the registered executable name. To enable the other samples,
run the corresponding command, e.g. eval "$(transcode.sh --completion bash)".

 Zsh

Initialize Zsh's completion system before registering the tool:

zsh
export PATH="$PWD/examples/scripts:$PATH"
autoload -Uz compinit
compinit
eval "$(plan.py --completion zsh)"


Put the same lines in ~/.zshrc, replacing $PWD with the absolute checkout
path. If your shell framework already runs compinit, add only the PATH and
eval lines after that initialization.

 Fish

In Fish, from the checkout root:

fish
fish_add_path "$PWD/examples/scripts"
mkdir -p ~/.config/fish/completions
plan.py --completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/plan.py.fish


Fish automatically loads that file for plan.py. For just the current session:

fish
plan.py --completion fish | source


The saved script asks the tool for its current declarations at completion time.
Repeat the install command for each tool, using its executable name as the filename.

 A directory of tools

The [dispatcher](applications.mddispatcher) also generates completion:

sh
clyops-dispatch --root ./examples/scripts --help
clyops-dispatch --root ./examples/scripts --name ops --completion bash


For convenient completion, use a wrapper that always supplies the root:

bash
!/usr/bin/env bash
exec clyops-dispatch --root /absolute/path/to/clyops/examples/scripts --name ops "$@"


Save this as an executable named ops on PATH. Enable it with
eval "$(ops --completion bash)", eval "$(ops --completion zsh)" after compinit,
or ops --completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/ops.fish.
The dispatcher completes directory groups and tool names, then the selected
tool's own options. Inspect ops --help for the command names it discovered.

 Inspect and troubleshoot

plan.py --completion bash prints shell source; plan.py --bash-completion
prints the tab-separated records the generated completion script consumes.
The internal protocol's historical name is used by all three shells.
Try command -v plan.py and plan.py --help if completion does not appear.
When using an interpreter directly, completion belongs to the tool's executable
name rather than a global python command; prefer an executable shebang script.
See the [shared behavior guide](guide.mdhelp-schema-and-shell-completion).

title: From script to agent
text:
From script to agent

The homepage follows a tiny tool called plan. It validates a service, an
environment and a replica count, then prints a JSON deployment plan. It changes
no infrastructure. The same example works in Python, Bash, TypeScript and Rust.

The animation is static illustrative playback. Help and tool results are captured
from the actual programs during the documentation build, which also calls each
variant through MCP and HTTP. The agent conversation is illustrative; it is not
a recorded Claude session. Schema and HTTP frames show selected fields to fit
the terminal. Browsers do not execute scripts or connect to an agent.

 Write the tool

Create a project directory with a scripts folder. Pick a language and install
its library using the corresponding guide:

| Language | Example source | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Python | [plan.py](/demos/plan.py) | [Python](languages/python.md) |
| Bash | [plan.sh](/demos/plan.sh) | [Bash](languages/bash.md) |
| TypeScript | [plan.ts](/demos/plan.ts) | [JavaScript / TypeScript](languages/javascript.md) |
| Rust | [plan.rs](/demos/plan.rs) | [Rust](languages/rust.md) |

These source downloads are generated website destinations. On GitHub, use
the [example directory](https://github.com/wankdanker/clyops/tree/main/docs/examples/home) instead.

For Python, install clyops, save plan.py in scripts, then:

sh
chmod +x scripts/plan.py
python scripts/plan.py --service api --env staging --replicas 2
python scripts/plan.py --help
python scripts/plan.py --help-json-schema


The plan is:

json
{"service": "api", "env": "staging", "replicas": 2}


The help text includes --service, --env and --replicas, defaults and accepted
values. --replicas 99 fails validation and exits with status 1. The schema
describes the same interface, the read-only effect and JSON stdout.

For Bash, put clyops.sh in the project root, save scripts/plan.sh and make it
executable. Run bash scripts/plan.sh with the same options. For TypeScript,
install clyops and tsx, save scripts/plan.ts, make it executable and run
pnpm exec tsx scripts/plan.ts. The TypeScript shebang uses env -S to launch
pnpm exec tsx when a server invokes the file directly. For Rust, put plan.rs
in a Cargo project's src/main.rs, add clyops with cargo add clyops, build
with cargo build --release, and copy the executable to scripts/plan.
Keep only your chosen variant in the served directory so it appears as one tool.

 Connect an agent

Install the Node adapters in the project root:

sh
pnpm add clyops-mcp clyops-api


Register the directory with Claude Code, then start a session:

sh
claude mcp add --transport stdio ops -- pnpm exec clyops-mcp --root ./scripts --read-only
claude


This uses Claude Code's [local stdio MCP configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcpoption-3-add-a-local-stdio-server).
Run from the project root; a client launched from another directory can use
absolute paths and pnpm --dir /absolute/project exec .... Follow the client's
connection and approval prompts. Other MCP clients can use pnpm as the command
with exec, clyops-mcp, --root and the absolute scripts directory as arguments.

An illustrative request is: “Plan two api replicas in staging.” The agent can call
the plan tool with this input:

json
{"service": "api", "env": "staging", "replicas": 2}


The server derives the tool's inputs from its schema, validates them, runs the
program and returns the plan. The tool's declared read-only effect becomes an
MCP annotation; --read-only filters the directory to tools declaring that effect.
See [MCP setup and behavior](node-tools.mdmcp) for the full interface.

 Serve the same tool over HTTP

In one terminal:

sh
pnpm exec clyops-api --root ./scripts --read-only


In another:

sh
curl localhost:8080/tools/plan \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"service":"api","env":"staging","replicas":2}'


The response includes ok, exitCode, the captured output and its parsed json
plan. /openapi.json describes the HTTP interface. See the [HTTP guide](node-tools.mdhttp-api)
for the complete response, authentication, filters, jobs and streamed I/O.

 Open the desktop runner

Install the runner from the [GitHub releases](https://github.com/wankdanker/clyops/releases)
and select the same scripts directory. It reads the schema to create fields for
service, environment and replica count, and streams the tool's output when you
run it. See the [desktop guide](applications.mddesktop-runner).

title: Clone-and-run example tools
text:
Clone-and-run example tools

The repository includes a mixed [scripts directory](../examples/scripts) that
works immediately after cloning. The Python tools use only the standard library;
the Bash wrappers use the library beside them in the checkout. You do not need
to build clyops or install a Python package first.

sh
git clone https://github.com/wankdanker/clyops.git
cd clyops
./examples/scripts/plan.py --help
./examples/scripts/plan.py --env production --replicas 3 --tag demo
./examples/scripts/report.py --format table
printf '{"z":2,"a":1}' | ./examples/scripts/json-format.py --sort


Use Python 3.9+ and Bash 4.3+. On macOS, use a current Bash from your package
manager; the system's Bash 3.2 is too old for the Bash library.

 Real wrappers, useful contracts

| Tool | Try it | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| plan.py | --env production --replicas 3 --tag demo | Choices, ranges, repeatable options, exclusive notification destinations |
| report.py | --format table --limit 75 --service worker | File validation, CSV processing, filtering, numeric bounds |
| json-format.py | --input examples/data/service.json --sort | Files or stdin, booleans, pretty/compact choice, JSON stdout |
| media-info.sh | examples/data/tone.wav | FFprobe metadata inspection |
| transcode.sh | examples/data/tone.wav /tmp/clyops-demo.m4a | FFmpeg command preview, quality range, encoder preset |
| upload.sh | examples/data/service.json --url https://example.com/upload | curl HTTP PUT preview, secret bearer token, bounded timeout |

Prefix these tool names with ./examples/scripts/, or add that directory to PATH.
The media tools need FFmpeg to execute; upload needs curl. Their generated help,
schema and completion work without those optional dependencies. Transcode and
upload preview by default; --execute performs the operation. Transcode refuses
to overwrite its output, and upload previews redact bearer tokens. The bundled
tone/CSV/JSON keep the walkthrough self-contained.

 The same scripts in the web runner

From the cloned repository:

sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm build
node apps/api/dist/cli.js --root ./examples/scripts --port 8788


Open http://127.0.0.1:8788/ui/. Select a Python tool to run immediately. Choices
become dropdowns, numeric ranges become bounded controls, and JSON-format exposes
stdin and file upload. Upload's token uses a secret field; network/destructive
effects prompt confirmation. Enable the wrapper's execute override to perform
its operation. Scripts execute on the API host and use its installed tools.

The scripts also work with the [MCP server](node-tools.mdmcp),
[dispatcher and desktop runner](applications.md).
See the [example directory README](../examples/README.md) for the full commands.

 Browser playground

The [Linux lab](linux-lab.md) runs all six scripts in a real Bash shell with
FFmpeg, curl, Python, pipes and completion. Transcode the bundled audio, upload
it to the guest's HTTP server, and download the result. You can add your own
small files; the workspace resets when you stop the lab. All execution stays
inside the browser, with no external network relay.

The [homepage playground](/playground) executes the real Python library and
plan.py, report.py, and json-format.py sources using
[Pyodide](https://pyodide.org/en/stable/usage/webworker.html). It loads Python only
when you press Start; the first load needs a network connection to the pinned
Pyodide CDN. Execution and the sample filesystem stay in a Web Worker in your tab.

Try plan.py --help, plan.py --replicas 99, report.py --format table, or
plan.py --help-json-schema. cat examples/scripts/plan.py shows the source.
Tab completes commands/options/choices from the actual completion protocol;
Up/Down recall commands. The stdin panel supplies input for json-format.py.
Reset terminates the worker and restores the workspace when you start again.
ls labels the Bash files as source examples to run locally; cat lets you
read them here, and attempting to run one explains which runtime is needed.

This is a Python command playground, with help, ls, cat, pwd and clear.
It has no host shell, Bash, FFmpeg, curl, pipes or live agent connection. Run the
[Linux lab](linux-lab.md), local scripts or API for those workflows. The animated hero remains an
[illustrative walkthrough](demo.md); the playground performs real executions.

title: Concepts and behavior
text:
Concepts and behavior

The APIs use native naming conventions, with the same underlying behavior.
The [language guides](reference.md) show their signatures and runnable programs.
This guide uses JavaScript spelling for recipes; register everything before run().

 Register options and arguments

javascript
cli.opt('PORT', 'port', 'p', '8080', 'Server port', 'Network', 'port');
cli.opt('VERBOSE', 'verbose', 'v', 'flag', 'Verbose output');
cli.opt('TOKEN', 'token', '', '', 'Required token', 'Auth', 'secret');
cli.optArray('TAG', 'tag', 't', 'Repeatable tags');
cli.arg('INPUT', 'Input file', '', 'file:exists');
cli.argVariadic('EXTRA', 'Additional input files', 'file:exists');


| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| variable | Key in resolved values and the environment variable name, e.g. PORT |
| long | Long option without --, e.g. port |
| short | Single-character alias without -; empty means no alias |
| default | Literal default, flag, optional, or empty for a required option |
| description | Text shown in help and the schema |
| group | Help section; defaults to Options |
| rule | Validation rule; empty means text |

Repeatable options accumulate CLI values; positional arguments are assigned in
registration order. A variadic must be last. An empty positional default makes
it required. A CLI level contains positionals or subcommands, not both.

| Operation | JS / Java | Python / Ruby | Rust | Go | Bash / C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Option | opt | opt | opt | Opt | clyops_opt |
| Repeatable option | optArray | opt_array | opt_array | OptArray | clyops_opt_array |
| Argument | arg | arg | arg | Arg | clyops_arg |
| Variadic | argVariadic | arg_variadic | arg_variadic | ArgVariadic | clyops_arg_variadic |

Rust puts option group and rule on the returned registration handle; C uses
designated metadata fields. See each native reference before translating a recipe.

 Values, precedence and flags

Precedence is command line → config → environment → default. Integer, float,
boolean and flag rules produce native typed values; arrays contain typed elements.
Unset optional values are null/nil/None or the language's documented empty value.

--verbose enables a flag; --no-verbose explicitly disables it and overrides an
enabled environment/config value. --verbose=false is also supported. Boolean
words are case insensitive: true/false, yes/no, 1/0, on/off.

source('port') reports cli, config, env, default or unset.
isSet asks whether it came from CLI; isExplicitlySet includes config and env.
Ruby uses set? and explicitly_set?; Bash/C use the clyops_ forms.
Typed getters may return a default for the wrong type; check presence/type when
that difference matters. Runtime registration does not infer application-specific
field types in TypeScript, Python or Ruby.

 Validation

Rules include int, float, bool, port, ip, hostname, url, email,
uuid, json, json:SCHEMA, date:YYYY-MM-DD, path, file:exists, file:readable, file:writable,
file:executable, dir:exists and dir:writable. Parameterized rules include int:1-10,
float:0-1, string:1-100, choice:red,green,blue and regex:PATTERN.
See [spec section 5](../spec/SPEC.md5-validation-rules) for ranges and exact behavior.

Use file:executable for an option that names a program to run (--ffmpeg): a bare
name must be on PATH and stays as given, and anything with a / must be an executable
file. It also tells servers that run tools for remote callers not to take that option
from them ([spec section 13](../spec/SPEC.md13-json-input-toargv)), and shells complete
command names for it.

Use json for an option that takes structured data (--meta '{"lang": "en"}'): the
value must be one JSON value, and stays the text as given for the program to parse.
Every language checks it the same way, with no dependencies. Through the HTTP API and
MCP server a caller can send the object itself; it reaches the tool as JSON text.

json:SCHEMA adds the JSON Schema the value should match: inline
(json:{"type":"object","required":["lang"]}), a file relative to root
(json:schemas/meta.json), or a URL (json:https://example.com/meta.json). The program
still checks only that the value is JSON. The schema goes into --help-json-schema, a
file being read only then (a missing one is a warning, not an error), and the HTTP API
and MCP server check input against it before the tool runs. They don't fetch URLs: a
URL schema documents the input but isn't checked.

Standalone validate helpers return a typed value or the native validation
error/result. Unknown registration rules and duplicate names are programming
errors. Bad CLI values are parse errors. These are separate error paths.

 Parse without exiting

javascript
const result = cli.parse(['input.txt', '--port', '443']);
if (result.status === 'ok') console.log(cli.values.PORT);
else if (result.status === 'help') console.log(cli.usage());
else console.error(result.error);


run() handles help, schema, completion and process exit; parse() returns a
native outcome. Read values after success. Parsing resets prior invocation state.
Python/Ruby expose values; Rust has values(); Go has Values; Java has
values(). C returns CLYOPS_OK/HELP/ERROR and exposes clyops_error.
Bash returns zero on success and uses _CLYOPS_HELP or _CLYOPS_ERROR on failure;
call clyops_parse in an if when using set -e.

 Config files and paths

javascript
cli.opt('CONFIG', 'config', 'c', 'optional', 'Config file', 'Config', 'path');
cli.setConfig('config', 'send:');
cli.setPathSearch('input', ['assets', 'fixtures']);


The last line requires an option named input to have been registered. Config is
line-oriented: send:port=443, with @include relative-file for includes. Prefixes
select the program's keys; keys that aren't option names are ignored, so several
programs can share one file. --help-json-schema reports the declaration as
config ({"option": "config", "prefixes": ["send:"]}, or null), which is
how clyops-doc writes a FILES section.

CLI paths resolve against the working directory; config paths resolve against
the config file containing the value; default/environment paths resolve against
the CLI root. Paths are normalized after precedence. - denotes stdin where the
application supports it. Path validation does not itself open/read files for the
application. See [spec section 6](../spec/SPEC.md6-paths).

 Nested commands and constraints

javascript
const db = cli.command('db', 'Database tasks');
const migrate = db.command('migrate', 'Apply migrations');
migrate.opt('TO', 'to', '', 'optional', 'Target version', 'Options', 'int');
migrate.setEffects('destructive');
cli.opt('JSON', 'json', '', 'flag', 'JSON output');
cli.opt('QUIET', 'quiet', '', 'flag', 'Quiet output');
cli.exclusive('json', 'quiet');


Use this recipe on a CLI with no root positionals. Parent options are accepted
before or after command words. commandPath gives the selected words, e.g.
['db', 'migrate']; use the native accessor listed in the reference.
exclusive permits at most one listed option, requires(a, b...) means a given
a needs the others, and oneOf requires at least one. Register referenced
options first. Explicitly false flags do not count as given for relationships.

 Secrets, effects and streams

javascript
cli.opt('TOKEN', 'token', '', '', 'API token', 'Auth', 'secret');
cli.setEffects('network', 'idempotent');
cli.setStdin('Input document', 'application/json');
cli.setStdout('Result document', 'application/json');


secret and secret:RULE mask help/config previews and valuesJson(); the
application still receives the real value. Avoid printing it yourself.
Effects are read-only, idempotent, destructive and network.
stdin/stdout declarations describe your program; your code performs the actual
I/O. Schemas carry these declarations for API/MCP/desktop consumers.

 Roles on file descriptors

A program can offer streams beyond stdin, stdout and stderr, such as progress or
metadata, by declaring roles. The runner that starts it decides which it wants and
on which descriptors:

javascript
cli.role('meta', 'out', 'Transfer metadata, before the output', 'application/json');
cli.role('progress', 'out', 'Progress, one JSON object per line', 'application/x-ndjson');
cli.run();
cli.emit('meta', { name: 'clip.mp4' });
cli.emit('progress', { pct: 50 });


The names meta, progress, log and result mean the same to every runner;
any other name is free text. Roles show in help (Output [progress]: …) and as
roles in the schema, on the level they are registered on; commands inherit their
ancestors'.

The runner puts each descriptor at its number before starting the program and
lists the mapping in CLYOPS_FDS. Without it, emit does nothing, so a program
run by hand needs only stdin, stdout and stderr. To see progress in a terminal:

sh
CLYOPS_FDS=progress:2 mytool input.wav            progress on stderr
CLYOPS_FDS=progress:4 mytool input.wav 4>log.ndjson


The library reads CLYOPS_FDS once and removes it from the environment, so
programs yours starts don't inherit it by accident. To share a stream with one,
keep its descriptor open in the child and set the child's CLYOPS_FDS to
forwardFds('progress'). Streams of lines (progress, log) share well; meta
and result describe one program's output. fdOpen returns a role's descriptor
(or none), for reading an in role or writing raw bytes.

 Help, schema and shell completion

See [Bash, Zsh and Fish setup](completion.md) for startup files, PATH, sample tools
and completing a whole directory with the dispatcher.

Every standalone program supports --help, --help-json-schema, and
--completion bash|zsh|fish. For example:

sh
eval "$(mytool --completion bash)"


Use usage, jsonSchema, completionScript and completionData when embedding
the library. The schema format discriminator is clyops: 1. Completion follows
commands and their inherited options. valuesJson is a separate resolved-values
document, with secrets masked.

 Logging and helper functions

info, warn, error and success write timestamped messages to stderr. die
logs and exits with the supplied code. CLYOPS_SILENT=true or the native silent
setter suppresses ordinary logging; parse errors and die still print.
NO_COLOR disables colors. The Node, Go, Java and C helpers support their native
format arguments; Python/Ruby/Rust/Bash receive a rendered message.

Native references also cover rule descriptions, validation, path resolution,
text wrapping and value accessors where those helpers are public.

bash quickstart.sh --help-json-schema

 Validation error; exit status 1


 Editor support and resolved values

Bash Language Server can navigate sourced functions and their usage comments. Bash has no portable static type-declaration format. Use the reference for parameter conventions, array outputs and exit statuses.

 Commands, relationships, secrets, effects and I/O

Add these registrations before calling run. A CLI level has either subcommands or positional arguments.

bash
clyops_opt     TOKEN token t "" "API token" Auth secret    masked in help and clyops_values_json
clyops_exclusive json quiet                                also clyops_requires a b..., clyops_one_of a b...
clyops_stdin   "Audio to transcribe" audio/wav             and clyops_stdout description content-type
clyops_role    progress out "Progress" application/x-ndjson     then clyops_emit progress '{"pct":50}'
clyops_effects read-only                                   read-only, idempotent, destructive, network
clyops_command db "Database tasks"                         later registrations belong to db...
clyops_command "db migrate" "Apply migrations"             ...then to db migrate
clyops_opt     TO to "" optional "Target version" Options int

[spec](../../spec/SPEC.md) sections 1.3 to 1.7.

Registration errors (duplicate names, unknown rules, or commands mixed with positionals) are programming errors, distinct from invalid user input. Try the whole workflow

The guest starts in /workspace, with the example scripts on PATH and Bash
completion already enabled. This is an ordinary Linux shell: pipes, redirection,
history, environment variables, cat, ls and the programs' real help work here.

bash
ls examples/scripts
media-info.sh examples/data/tone.wav
transcode.sh examples/data/tone.wav /tmp/tone.m4a --execute
upload.sh /tmp/tone.m4a --url http://127.0.0.1:9000/upload --execute
plan.py --env production --replicas 3 | json-format.py --sort


Transcode produces an actual AAC audio file with FFmpeg. The upload sends a real
HTTP PUT through curl to a Python server inside this Linux guest. Its response
contains the received byte count, SHA-256 and saved path. Use the download button
to save the audio output to your computer. Scripts, validation and completion
come directly from this checkout's Bash/Python library and examples.

Files you add appear under /workspace/inbox/. For example, inspect one with
media-info.sh '/workspace/inbox/your file.wav'. You can freely edit the guest's
files and scripts; everything lives in memory for this session. Stop & reset
unloads the emulator, and Start restores a fresh guest.

 What runs where

[v86](https://github.com/copy/v86) emulates a 32-bit PC and executes Alpine Linux
and normal Linux binaries in a Web Worker. The website serves static assets;
it does not execute your commands on a server. No network relay is configured,
so the guest's upload server is reachable inside the guest and public internet
destinations are unavailable. The lab needs a connection to load its static
filesystem assets. Large files and long encodes are better run locally.

For a smaller download, the [Python playground](/playground) runs three of the
same examples directly in Pyodide. For your real filesystem and network,
[clone and run the scripts](examples.md) or use the [web runner](web-runner.md).

 Guest software and sources

The lab uses Alpine Linux packages with their individual upstream licenses.
[Package versions and licenses](/assets/linux-lab/packages.json) and the
[v86 license](/assets/linux-lab/v86-LICENSE.txt) ship with the assets.
The [guest build recipe](../tools/linux-lab) and [asset builder](../tools/build-linux-lab.py)
describe the image. The package index records each origin's Alpine source commit
and upstream project; corresponding Alpine build recipes and source patches are
in [Alpine aports](https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports).

title: Maintaining the documentation
text:
Maintaining the documentation

 Build and preview

The full site build runs on Linux or macOS and uses Markdown guides and native
API references. Install Node 20.19+ (22.12+ for Node 22),
pnpm (the version pinned in package.json), Python 3.10+, Rust, Go 1.21+,
Java 17+/Maven, Ruby 3.3+, Doxygen and Graphviz (dot). The Linux lab guest also
requires Docker with Linux/386 image support (native on Linux x86; Docker Desktop
needs its x86 emulation support on ARM). These are documentation build requirements;
the supported library runtime versions remain those in each language guide.

sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
python3 -m venv .venv-docs
. .venv-docs/bin/activate
pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
gem install yard -v 0.9.38 --no-document
gem install rbs -v 3.4.0 --no-document
pnpm docs:build
pnpm docs:serve


docs:build builds Node packages, native references, compiled/executed examples,
then the site into _site, and validates local links and fragments.
docs:serve previews the previously generated references and watches Markdown
changes. Re-run the full build after changing public interfaces or native comments.
DOCS_PATH_PREFIX=/clyops/ pnpm docs:build validates a GitHub project-site build.
DOCS_PATH_PREFIX=/ pnpm docs:build builds for a custom domain such as clyops.io.

 Content and public interfaces

- docs/languages/.md: installation, runnable quickstart, native usage and editor setup.
- docs/guide.md: shared behavior and recipes, linked to the specification.
- docs/examples: runnable sources plus installed-consumer typing examples.
- Source comments/docstrings: API descriptions used by editors and native generators.
- packages/ruby/sig/clyops.rbs: type signatures shipped in the Ruby gem.

Keep guides as ordinary Markdown. Website navigation/layout are applied by
Eleventy; Markdown examples containing template syntax are not evaluated as templates.
Local Markdown links work in the repository and are translated for the website.
Generated native reference links point to website output, as explained in the
[reference index](reference.md). Source/spec links lead to GitHub.

The homepage uses docs/_includes/home.njk and the static CSS/JS in docs/assets.
Its playback is generated by tools/build-home-demo.mjs from executable examples
in docs/examples/home: all four variants are checked through the CLI, MCP and
HTTP before their captured output is used. Agent dialogue is illustrative;
schema and HTTP frames show labeled excerpts. That playback does not execute tools.
Playback pauses offscreen/in background tabs, supports manual language/step
selection, and starts paused when reduced motion is requested. A Markdown
[walkthrough](demo.md) provides readable setup instructions without animation.

The separate homepage playground runs the real Python examples and library in a
module Web Worker using Pyodide 314.0.7, loaded from its pinned CDN only on Start.
tools/build-playground.mjs packages checkout sources into an ignored JSON asset;
tools/playground.py dispatches commands, redirects streams and queries the
actual completion protocol. The sample scripts live in examples/scripts and
use examples/data. The docs build runs tools/test-examples.py, including
wrapper previews and argument handling with fake FFmpeg/curl commands.
pnpm test:docs-browser tests actual browser execution, lazy loading, input,
completion, reset and mobile layout. Run it after generating the static site;
use PLAYWRIGHT_CHANNEL=chrome for an installed Chrome. It needs network access
to the Pyodide CDN and leaves no server running after completion.

The [Linux lab](linux-lab.md) runs Alpine Linux in a v86 Web Worker with 256 MiB
of guest RAM. It boots only on Start and is terminated on reset or page exit.
tools/linux-lab builds ordinary Bash/Python/FFmpeg/curl binaries and a loopback
upload server into a Docker image. tools/build-linux-lab.py exports that image,
adds the checkout's examples and libraries, and generates a lazy 9p filesystem.
tools/build-linux-lab.mjs bundles xterm and the worker. The full docs build runs
both; for frontend edits, use pnpm docs:lab:build followed by pnpm docs:serve.
Activate the docs Python environment first. Docker is needed only when the guest
recipe changes; exported guests and verified BIOS files are cached under
.docs-tools/linux-lab, including in CI. Rebuilds always inject current example
sources. Generated assets are ignored by Git.

Guest files are compressed and addressed by their SHA-256. Publishing merges
them into a shared linux-runtime/ store at the Pages root so release snapshots
retain their dependencies without duplicating the entire guest. Browser bundles
and filesystem manifests remain specific to each snapshot. The lab configures
no external network relay; its real HTTP upload stays inside the guest. Browser
tests run one at a time and exercise Bash, FFprobe, FFmpeg, curl, pipes, file
transfers, reset, lazy loading and startup failures.

When adding or changing a public method, document its behavior, parameters,
return value, errors and an example where useful. Include ownership/lifetime
for C and process-exit behavior for parsing APIs. Public includes supported
constructors, properties, helpers and deprecated aliases; private implementation
methods are excluded. Native references retain the platform's standard-library
inherited API.

Quickstart fences marked <!-- example: filename --> must match the corresponding
source exactly. The build executes default, valid, invalid, help and schema cases
against all nine implementations. Rust additionally runs its native doctests in
the test suite. Generated folders are ignored and rebuilt, not committed.

 Checks and package artifacts

pnpm docs:check checks Python docstrings, Java/Bash public comments, Node exports
using the TypeScript compiler, and Markdown example synchronization. The full
build also validates TypeDoc references, rustdoc missing docs/links, Doxygen,
Go public comments, Ruby public methods/RBS, and static HTML links.

Installed-consumer checks pack all six public Node packages and compile a TypeScript
consumer against their exported declarations. Declaration maps must resolve to
source files included in each tarball, so editor navigation works after installation.
The Python wheel is installed
into an isolated directory and checked with mypy; its py.typed marker is required.
Java artifacts must contain sources and Javadocs. Ruby gems must include signatures.
Ruby's existing runtime tests also run with RBS argument/result checking enabled.
Registry READMEs provide the quickstart and link here; the full guides and API
references live on the documentation site.

 Deployment and versions

The Docs workflow builds and checks pull requests, uploads a preview artifact,
and deploys successful main builds to GitHub Pages. Generated output is stored
on docs-pages so release snapshots survive future deployments and artifact expiry.
In repository Settings →
Pages, choose GitHub Actions as the source. No custom domain is required.
The workflow reads the configured Pages URL before building and uses its path
for assets, navigation, search and publishing. A custom domain such as
https://clyops.io/ uses /; a GitHub project URL uses /clyops/.
After changing the Pages custom domain, run Docs again to rebuild the links.
Until Pages is configured, the workflow completes its checks and uploads the
site artifact, then skips deployment. Enable Pages and run Docs again to publish.
Allow main and release tags in the github-pages environment's deployment rules
if that environment restricts branches/tags.

Tag builds also retain an immutable copy at versions/vX.Y.Z/, and update a
version index linked from the site. A release snapshot comes from its tag,
including the package versions and source comments. Do not edit an existing tag
to change old documentation. Use a new release for corrections to shipped docs.
The root site follows main; the displayed package version can contain changes
that have not yet been published to a registry.
tools/version.py set also updates versioned install examples in the guides and
the Java README. The static Markdown and its release artifacts stay in step.

 Web runner checks

The Web runner workflow runs the static SvelteKit build and browser tests against
a real authenticated API and executable tools. Locally, pnpm test:web uses a
Playwright Chromium installation; PLAYWRIGHT_CHANNEL=chrome pnpm test:web uses
an installed Chrome. Schema conversion has browser-bundle checks; API tests check
that UI assets ship and load without weakening tool/job authentication. The private
web app is copied into the public API package and is not packed/published separately.

title: Node tools, jobs, API and MCP
text:
Node tools, jobs, API and MCP

These packages expose native TypeScript declarations. Tools and jobs support
CommonJS and ESM; API and MCP use ESM. The
[Node reference](/reference/node/index.html) lists every published export, including
interfaces, helpers, queue methods and server lifecycle functions.

 Discover and invoke tools

sh
pnpm add clyops-tools


javascript
const { loadTools, runTool } = require('clyops-tools');
const loaded = await loadTools('/path/to/tools');
const tool = loaded.tools.find(t => t.words.join(' ') === 'send');
if (!tool) throw new Error('send was not discovered');
const result = await runTool(tool, { SRC: 'input.txt', host: 'example.com' }, {
  timeoutMs: 5000,
});
if (!result.ok) console.error(result.stderr);


Run this inside an async function in CommonJS, or use ESM imports and top-level
await. discover builds the tree without execution; loadSchema probes recognized
tools; loadTools loads schemas (8 probes at a time, 30 s each, set with
concurrency and timeoutMs) and expands leaf commands. watchTools reloads
changed tools and has current() and close(); close it during shutdown.

toArgv maps input using the tool schema. It reports unknown/controlled keys;
callers decide whether those are errors. Positionals come first by default;
dash-prefixed values follow options and --. positionals: 'last' changes their
order. secretEnv passes scalar secrets in the environment; within restricts
path input. toJsonSchema describes accepted input; redactArgv masks secrets
in displayed commands. See [spec section 13](../spec/SPEC.md13-json-input-toargv).

A server taking input over a network decides which inputs callers may set
(spec section 13): closedInputs(schema, { confined, allowExecutables }) names
the closed ones (file:executable unless allowed, and path inputs unless
confined), publicSchema(schema, closed) is the schema callers should see,
closedKeys finds input that sets one, and closedRequirement names a required
argument that is closed, so the tool can't be served. Pass closed to
runTool/startTool and input setting one is an InputError.

 Streams, cancellation and errors

run(file, argv, options) resolves a RunResult; nonzero exit codes are outcomes,
while spawn/input/output stream errors reject. start additionally returns the
child and readable stdout. stdin accepts text, Buffer or Readable.
stdout: 'buffer' captures binary data; 'stream' exposes it for consumption.
Use timeoutMs, signal and maxOutput to bound execution. Await the result
promise, consume streamed stdout, and handle rejected promises. Timeout/abort
sends the process tree SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after killGraceMs (default 200),
and cleans up streams. On Windows the tree is stopped at once, without a grace period.

roles wires up a tool's [roles](guide.mdroles-on-file-descriptors) for one run:
each named role gets the next descriptor from 3, the tool is told in CLYOPS_FDS,
output roles are collected into the result's roles and passed line by line to
onLine, and input roles are fed like stdin. startTool and runTool keep only
the roles a tool declares, so asking every tool for progress is safe:

javascript
const result = await runTool(tool, input, { roles: { progress: { onLine: (l) => show(JSON.parse(l)) }, meta: {} } });
result.roles?.meta; // the tool's meta document, as text


runTool adds schema mapping, secret handling and ok. Filters (allow, deny,
readOnly) and path boundaries should match the application's intended access.
auditLog provides an append-only JSONL audit writer. See the
[tools package guide](../packages/tools/README.md).

 Jobs and templates

sh
pnpm add clyops-jobs


javascript
const { JobQueue } = require('clyops-jobs');
const queue = new JobQueue({ concurrency: 2, keep: 100 });
const job = queue.add('example', async ({ signal, stage }) => {
  signal.throwIfAborted();
  stage('working');
  return { message: 'done' };
});
console.log(await job.done);
console.log(queue.get(job.record.job_id)?.record.status);


resolveFunctionConfig resolves a configured script and merges defaults/overrides;
buildFunctionCommand renders arguments; runScriptFunction executes it with
optional stdin/stdout files. A function run wires the tool's progress, meta and
log roles (onProgress, the run's meta), and queue tasks record progress with
progress(update). Templates use dotted paths in ${expression} or
{{expression}}. Boolean templates are validated after rendering. A missing
params field leaves an option or positional that names it unset, even inside a
longer string, instead of failing the job (a function's strict_params: true makes
it an error); other unknown paths are errors.

Artifact helpers discover, inspect and copy output files. Record helpers create
and transition serializable job states. JobQueue.add returns a cancellation
method and a done promise; get and list expose retained work. Cancellation
is recorded as an error with cancelled; onDrop lets the host clean retained
files. The queue is in memory, so durable storage is the host's responsibility.
See [job configuration and artifacts](../packages/jobs/README.md).

 HTTP API

sh
pnpm add clyops-api
pnpm exec clyops-api --root ./tools --port 8080 --read-only


javascript
import { createApi } from 'clyops-api';
const api = await createApi({ root: './tools', watch: true, timeoutMs: 5000 });
const server = api.app.listen(8080);
// During shutdown: server.close(); api.close();


The API serves a [static web runner](web-runner.md) at /ui/; ui: false or
--no-ui disables it. The API exposes tool endpoints, OpenAPI, asynchronous job records and optional
MCP transport. Options include named scoped keys, filters, path boundaries,
body/output limits, concurrency, audit and hot reload. Binary output and streamed
stdin have transport-specific conventions. A tool's meta and progress roles show
up in the JSON envelope, on job records, as GET /jobs/<id>/events server-sent
events and as an X-Clyops-Meta header on streamed output; see the [HTTP guide](../apps/api/README.md)
for routes and examples. toZod is the exported input-validator adapter.

 MCP

sh
pnpm add clyops-mcp
pnpm exec clyops-mcp --root ./tools


createMcpServer adapts loaded tools to an MCP server; mcpHttpHandler installs
streamable HTTP transport in an HTTP host; toolName derives exposed names.
Effects become annotations. The server exposes declared stdin and represents
binary output as image/audio/blob results. A tool's progress role becomes MCP
progress notifications when the request has a progress token, and its meta comes
back in the result's _meta. See the [MCP guide](../apps/mcp/README.md)
for transport setup and lifecycle responsibilities.

title: Web runner and shared schema
text:
Web runner and shared schema

The SvelteKit web runner turns the REST API's tool descriptions into forms and
execution results. Its built HTML/CSS/JavaScript are static, packaged with the API,
and served at /ui/. It does not need a SvelteKit server at runtime.

 Start and connect

Install clyops-api and start it with your executable scripts directory:

sh
pnpm add clyops-api
pnpm exec clyops-api --root ./scripts --api-key YOUR_KEY


Open http://localhost:8080/ui/, enter the key, and connect. The UI shell is public
so it can present the login controls; every API tool/job request still requires
the configured key. --no-ui disables the bundled frontend independently.
From this repository, pnpm build builds the shared package, SPA and API in order;
node apps/api/dist/cli.js --root ./scripts starts the built server.

The connection URL is the API root, not its /ui/ path. Keys stay in memory and
are cleared from the password input after connecting. Disconnect clears the client.
API key scopes continue to determine which tools and jobs are visible.

The default same-origin deployment needs no CORS setup. A frontend served from
another origin requires explicit CORS support in the API's reverse proxy, including
Authorization/Content-Type headers, OPTIONS and GET/POST/DELETE. Use an HTTPS API
when the frontend is HTTPS. The documentation site remains a separate static site;
it does not run the tools or host a REST backend.

 Forms and inheritance

Select a tool from its directory group. Commands appear as separate leaf tools,
with inherited registrations already expanded by the API.

| Declaration | Form control |
| --- | --- |
| choice:a,b | Enum dropdown |
| Integer range | Number input with min/max and step 1 |
| Float range | Number input with min/max and arbitrary fractional step |
| String length | Length-aware text input |
| Repeatable option or variadic argument | Repeatable, typed item controls |
| Boolean | Inherit/on/off |
| Secret | Password control, excluded from previews and templates |
| Path | Server path input with optional file upload |
| Declared stdin | Text or file input |
| Declared binary stdout | Authenticated download |

Only enabled overrides are submitted. Declared defaults are hints; they are not
automatically sent. Explicit zero and false are preserved. Untouched values are
resolved by the tool from config, environment and defaults using the usual
[precedence rules](guide.md).

Relationship summaries explain exclusive, requires and oneOf. clyops
oneOf means at least one; combine it with exclusive for exactly one. Explicit
exclusive conflicts block submission. Requirements that may be satisfied by
config/environment are advisory, and the tool validates effective values.
Destructive tools require confirmation before execution.

The JSON editor applies the same input schema as the API. It omits secrets;
password values remain in their dedicated controls. Templates save only known,
non-secret overrides in this browser, scoped by API and tool. Files and stdin are
not saved, and restoring a template clears secret fields.

 Execution and jobs

Run synchronously for a result, or submit a background job and follow its status.
The runner polls the existing job endpoints and supports cancellation. A job whose
tool declares a progress role shows a progress bar while it runs; output is shown
when the job finishes, with the tool's meta beside it. This interface does not
promise live log streaming.
stdout and stderr render ANSI colors (basic, 256-color and truecolor) and styles
by default. Uncheck ANSI colors for plain text without escape sequences.
Output remains escaped text; terminal hyperlinks and cursor instructions are
ignored. This is a captured log view rather than an interactive terminal.
Tools must emit ANSI codes; tools that disable color when piped need their own
color option enabled. Downloads preserve original output bytes. Parsed JSON is
displayed as text. Binary envelopes and job
output are downloaded with the API client's bearer key, without putting the key
into a download URL. See [REST endpoints](node-tools.mdhttp-api).

 Shared library

clyops-schema is a dependency-free, browser-compatible package with types,
toJsonSchema, valueSchema, name mapping, formFields, formSchema,
constraintIssues, withoutSecrets and isTextType. The
[complete Node API reference](/reference/node/index.html) documents its exports.

ts
import { toJsonSchema, formFields, constraintIssues } from 'clyops-schema';
const inputSchema = toJsonSchema(toolSchema);
const controls = formFields(toolSchema);
const relationships = constraintIssues(toolSchema, overrides);


toJsonSchema(schema, 'declared') keeps the original keys for desktop templates;
the default uses the API/MCP input keys. formSchema adds clyops metadata without
changing request validation. The API and MCP retain their existing clyops-tools
imports, which re-export the shared converter for compatibility. The desktop
editor now uses it too, and numeric fields share the range conversion.

Build/type/test commands and browser checks are in the [app README](../apps/web/README.md).
